translations.title: Build It
translations.explanation: Build It is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Constructions and Rigid Transformations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-CO.A.1, CCSS:HSG-CO.D.12. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Know precise definitions of angle, circle, perpendicular line, parallel line, and line segment, based on the undefined notions of point, line, distance along a line, and distance around a circular arc. Make formal geometric constructions with a variety of tools and methods (compass and straightedge, string, reflective devices, paper folding, dynamic geometric software, etc.). Copying a segment; copying an angle; bisecting a segment; bisecting an angle; constructing perpendicular lines, including the perpendicular bisector of a line segment; and constructing a line parallel to a given line through a point not on the line. Instructional focus: Students reason with rigid transformations, constructions, congruence criteria, and geometric proof. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Build It. Translations, rotations, and reflections preserve distance and angle measure. Congruence can be established by a sequence of rigid motions or valid triangle-congruence criteria.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Translate point P(4,6) by vector ⟨2,4⟩. The image is P′(6,10); the translation preserves distances and angle measures. Example 2: Translate point P(6,5) by vector ⟨4,4⟩. The image is P′(10,9); the translation preserves distances and angle measures.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add 2 to the x-coordinate: 4+2=6. Step 2: add 4 to the y-coordinate: 6+4=10. Step 3: record P′(6,10). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid. Step 1: add 4 to the x-coordinate: 6+4=10. Step 2: add 4 to the y-coordinate: 5+4=9. Step 3: record P′(10,9). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Build It. Do not treat dilation as a rigid motion unless the scale factor has magnitude 1. A diagram alone does not prove congruence; cite preserved properties or a theorem.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Build It. Describe the transformation or given properties, apply a valid congruence argument, and justify each conclusion rather than relying on appearance.

Theorems include: opposite sides are congruent, opposite angles are congruent, the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and conversely, rectangles are parallelograms with congruent diagonals. translations.title: Practicing Proofs
translations.explanation: Practicing Proofs is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Congruence”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-MG.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply geometric methods to solve design problems (e.g., designing an object or structure to satisfy physical constraints or minimize cost; working with typographic grid systems based on ratios).★ Instructional focus: Students apply geometric shapes, measures, scale, density, and constraints to model real objects and design decisions. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Practicing Proofs. Choose an idealized shape that captures the relevant features, define units, state assumptions, calculate with geometric measures, and evaluate whether the approximation is suitable.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A cylinder with radius 5 and height 8 has volume V=πr²h=π(5²)(8)=200π cubic units, about 628.32. Example 2: A cylinder with radius 4 and height 8 has volume V=πr²h=π(4²)(8)=128π cubic units, about 402.12.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify radius r=5 and height h=8. Step 2: square the radius: 5²=25. Step 3: multiply by height: 25×8=200. Step 4: volume is 200π≈628.32 cubic units. Step 1: identify radius r=4 and height h=8. Step 2: square the radius: 4²=16. Step 3: multiply by height: 16×8=128. Step 4: volume is 128π≈402.12 cubic units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Practicing Proofs. Do not claim false precision from an approximate geometric model. Distinguish linear scale from area or volume scale.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Practicing Proofs. Model the relevant geometry, calculate with consistent units, interpret the result, and discuss the assumptions or approximation.

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply geometric methods to solve design problems (e.g., designing an object or structure to satisfy physical constraints or minimize cost; working with typographic grid systems based on ratios).★ Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi- step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Scale of the Solar System. Choose an idealized shape that captures the relevant features, define units, state assumptions, calculate with geometric measures, and evaluate whether the approximation is suitable.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A cylinder with radius 6 and height 9 has volume V=πr²h=π(6²)(9)=324π cubic units, about 1017.88. Example 2: A cylinder with radius 3 and height 6 has volume V=πr²h=π(3²)(6)=54π cubic units, about 169.65.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify radius r=6 and height h=9. Step 2: square the radius: 6²=36. Step 3: multiply by height: 36×9=324. Step 4: volume is 324π≈1017.88 cubic units. Step 1: identify radius r=3 and height h=6. Step 2: square the radius: 3²=9. Step 3: multiply by height: 9×6=54. Step 4: volume is 54π≈169.65 cubic units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Scale of the Solar System. Do not claim false precision from an approximate geometric model. Distinguish linear scale from area or volume scale.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Scale of the Solar System. Model the relevant geometry, calculate with consistent units, interpret the result, and discuss the assumptions or approximation.

translations.title: Are They All Similar?
translations.explanation: Are They All Similar? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Similarity”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-C.A.1, CCSS:HSG-SRT.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Prove that all circles are similar. Given two figures, use the definition of similarity in terms of similarity transformations to decide if the y are similar; explain using similarity transformations the meaning of similarity for triangles as the equality of all corresponding pairs of angles and the proportionality of all corresponding pairs of sides. Instructional focus: Students connect central angles, arcs, chords, tangents, inscribed angles, and circle equations through geometric relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Are They All Similar?. A central angle has the same degree measure as its intercepted arc. An inscribed angle measures half its intercepted arc. A radius to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A central angle of 70° intercepts an arc of 70°. An inscribed angle intercepting that same arc measures 35°. Example 2: A central angle of 80° intercepts an arc of 80°. An inscribed angle intercepting that same arc measures 40°.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: central-angle measure equals intercepted arc measure, so the arc is 70°. Step 2: an inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc. Step 3: 70/2=35°. Step 4: verify the inscribed angle is smaller than the corresponding central angle. Step 1: central-angle measure equals intercepted arc measure, so the arc is 80°. Step 2: an inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc. Step 3: 80/2=40°. Step 4: verify the inscribed angle is smaller than the corresponding central angle.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Are They All Similar?. Do not confuse arc length with arc measure. Do not apply an inscribed-angle relationship to a central angle. Check whether the given line is actually tangent before using perpendicularity.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Are They All Similar?. Identify the circle elements and intercepted arc, apply the correct angle, length, tangent, or equation relationship, and verify the geometry.

translations.title: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem
translations.explanation: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Similarity”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-CED.A.4, CCSS:HSG-SRT.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Rearrange formulas to highlight a quantity of interest, using the same reasoning as in solving equations. For example, rearrange Ohm’s law V = IR to highlight resistance R. Prove theorems about triangles. Theorems include: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two proportionally, and conversely; the Pythagorean Theorem proved using triangle similarity. Instructional focus: Students define variables and create equations or inequalities that model relationships among quantities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem. Define each variable with units, translate each relationship before solving, and keep the equation dimensionally and contextually consistent. Rearranging a formula must use equivalent operations.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A situation has fixed amount 7 and increases by 3 per unit. Model it by y=3x+7. At x=6, y=25. Example 2: A situation has fixed amount 21 and increases by 4 per unit. Model it by y=4x+21. At x=2, y=29.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 3x. Step 3: add fixed amount 7. Step 4: substitute x=6: y=3(6)+7=25. Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 4x. Step 3: add fixed amount 21. Step 4: substitute x=2: y=4(2)+21=29.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem. Do not start manipulating symbols before stating what they mean. Avoid mixing total quantities with rates or per-unit quantities without the correct factor.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem. Define variables, translate the relationship, form an equation or inequality, and check that the model and units match the situation.

translations.title: Approximating Pi
translations.explanation: Approximating Pi is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Right Triangle Trigonometry”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-GMD.A.1, CCSS:HSN-Q.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Give an informal argument for the formulas for the circumference of a circle, area of a circle, volume of a cylinder, pyramid, and cone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Approximating Pi. Area uses square units and volume uses cubic units. Scaling all lengths by k scales area by k^2 and volume by k^3. Cross-sections depend on the plane cutting the solid.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A cylinder with radius 4 and height 5 has volume V=πr²h=π(4²)(5)=80π cubic units, about 251.33. Example 2: A cylinder with radius 6 and height 7 has volume V=πr²h=π(6²)(7)=252π cubic units, about 791.68.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify radius r=4 and height h=5. Step 2: square the radius: 4²=16. Step 3: multiply by height: 16×5=80. Step 4: volume is 80π≈251.33 cubic units. Step 1: identify radius r=6 and height h=7. Step 2: square the radius: 6²=36. Step 3: multiply by height: 36×7=252. Step 4: volume is 252π≈791.68 cubic units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Approximating Pi. Do not use a surface-area formula when volume is requested. Track whether a dimension is radius or diameter and keep units consistent.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Approximating Pi. Identify the geometric quantity and dimensions, apply the appropriate formula or scaling relationship, calculate, and state squared or cubed units correctly.

translations.title: Rigid Transformations in the Plane
translations.explanation: Rigid Transformations in the Plane is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Coordinate Geometry”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-CO.A.2, CCSS:HSG-CO.A.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Represent transformations in the plane using, e.g., transparencies and geometry software; describe transformations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give other points as outputs. Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle to those that do not (e.g., translation versus horizontal stretch). Given a geometric figure and a rotation, reflection, or translation, draw the transformed figure using, e.g., graph paper, tracing paper, or geometry software. Specify a sequence of transformations that will carry a given figure onto another. Instructional focus: Students reason with rigid transformations, constructions, congruence criteria, and geometric proof. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Rigid Transformations in the Plane. Translations, rotations, and reflections preserve distance and angle measure. Congruence can be established by a sequence of rigid motions or valid triangle-congruence criteria.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Translate point P(1,1) by vector ⟨3,2⟩. The image is P′(4,3); the translation preserves distances and angle measures. Example 2: Translate point P(6,6) by vector ⟨5,5⟩. The image is P′(11,11); the translation preserves distances and angle measures.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add 3 to the x-coordinate: 1+3=4. Step 2: add 2 to the y-coordinate: 1+2=3. Step 3: record P′(4,3). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid. Step 1: add 5 to the x-coordinate: 6+5=11. Step 2: add 5 to the y-coordinate: 6+5=11. Step 3: record P′(11,11). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Rigid Transformations in the Plane. Do not treat dilation as a rigid motion unless the scale factor has magnitude 1. A diagram alone does not prove congruence; cite preserved properties or a theorem.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Rigid Transformations in the Plane. Describe the transformation or given properties, apply a valid congruence argument, and justify each conclusion rather than relying on appearance.

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically. For example, prove or disprove that a figure defined by four given points in the coordinate plane is a rectangle; prove or disprove that the point (1, √3) lies on the circle centered at the origin and containing the point (0, 2). Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point). Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi- step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays. Instructional focus: Students use coordinates and algebra to describe geometric objects, prove relationships, and calculate distances, slopes, and equations. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Parallel Lines in the Plane. Slope represents direction and rate of change. Parallel nonvertical lines have equal slopes; perpendicular nonvertical lines have slopes whose product is -1. Distance and midpoint formulas follow from coordinate differences.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: y-change is 6=6. Step 2: x-change is 4=4. Step 3: slope is 6/4=3/2. Step 4: keep the subtraction order consistent for both coordinates. Step 1: y-change is 5=5. Step 2: x-change is 3=3. Step 3: slope is 5/3=5/3. Step 4: keep the subtraction order consistent for both coordinates.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Parallel Lines in the Plane. Do not divide by zero when a line is vertical. Keep x- and y-differences paired in the same order when calculating slope.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Parallel Lines in the Plane. Translate the geometry into coordinates, calculate the needed algebraic quantity, and interpret the result as a geometric property.

translations.title: Geometria analityczna — Parallel Lines in the Plane

Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Geometria analityczna — Parallel Lines in the Plane. Nachylenie opisuje kierunek i tempo zmian. Równoległe niepionowe proste mają równe współczynniki kierunkowe, a dla prostych prostopadłych ich iloczyn wynosi -1. Wzory na odległość i środek odcinka wynikają z różnic współrzędnych.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dla A(2,4) i B(6,10) współczynnik kierunkowy = (10-4)/(6-2) = 3/2. Przykład 2: Dla A(1,4) i B(4,9) współczynnik kierunkowy = (9-4)/(4-1) = 5/3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zmiana y: 6=6. Krok 2: zmiana x: 4=4. Krok 3: nachylenie 6/4=3/2. Krok 4: zachowaj tę samą kolejność odejmowania współrzędnych. Krok 1: zmiana y: 5=5. Krok 2: zmiana x: 3=3. Krok 3: nachylenie 5/3=5/3. Krok 4: zachowaj tę samą kolejność odejmowania współrzędnych.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Geometria analityczna — Parallel Lines in the Plane. Nie dziel przez zero dla prostej pionowej. Przy obliczaniu nachylenia zachowaj tę samą kolejność różnic współrzędnych x i y.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Geometria analityczna — Parallel Lines in the Plane. Przełóż problem geometryczny na współrzędne, oblicz potrzebną wielkość algebraiczną i zinterpretuj wynik jako własność geometryczną.

translations.title: Perpendicular Lines in the Plane
translations.explanation: Perpendicular Lines in the Plane is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Coordinate Geometry”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-CO.A.2, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.5, CCSS:HSN-Q.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Represent transformations in the plane using, e.g., transparencies and geometry software; describe transformations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give other points as outputs. Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle to those that do not (e.g., translation versus horizontal stretch). Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point). Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi- step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays. Instructional focus: Students reason with rigid transformations, constructions, congruence criteria, and geometric proof. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Perpendicular Lines in the Plane. Translations, rotations, and reflections preserve distance and angle measure. Congruence can be established by a sequence of rigid motions or valid triangle-congruence criteria.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Translate point P(3,6) by vector ⟨4,4⟩. The image is P′(7,10); the translation preserves distances and angle measures. Example 2: Translate point P(6,5) by vector ⟨3,5⟩. The image is P′(9,10); the translation preserves distances and angle measures.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add 4 to the x-coordinate: 3+4=7. Step 2: add 4 to the y-coordinate: 6+4=10. Step 3: record P′(7,10). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid. Step 1: add 3 to the x-coordinate: 6+3=9. Step 2: add 5 to the y-coordinate: 5+5=10. Step 3: record P′(9,10). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Perpendicular Lines in the Plane. Do not treat dilation as a rigid motion unless the scale factor has magnitude 1. A diagram alone does not prove congruence; cite preserved properties or a theorem.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Perpendicular Lines in the Plane. Describe the transformation or given properties, apply a valid congruence argument, and justify each conclusion rather than relying on appearance.

translations.title: Przystawanie i przekształcenia — Perpendicular Lines in the Plane
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Przystawanie i przekształcenia — Perpendicular Lines in the Plane” należy do działu „Coordinate Geometry” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:HSG-CO.A.2, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.5, CCSS:HSN-Q.A.1. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Przystawanie i przekształcenia — Perpendicular Lines in the Plane. Przesunięcia, obroty i odbicia zachowują odległości oraz miary kątów. Przystawanie można wykazać przez ciąg izometrii albo poprawne kryteria przystawania trójkątów.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Przesuń punkt P(3,6) o wektor ⟨4,4⟩. Obraz to P′(7,10); przesunięcie zachowuje odległości i kąty. Przykład 2: Przesuń punkt P(6,5) o wektor ⟨3,5⟩. Obraz to P′(9,10); przesunięcie zachowuje odległości i kąty.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: x: 3+4=7. Krok 2: y: 6+4=10. Krok 3: zapisz P′(7,10). Krok 4: wszystkie punkty przesunięto o ten sam wektor, więc jest to izometria. Krok 1: x: 6+3=9. Krok 2: y: 5+5=10. Krok 3: zapisz P′(9,10). Krok 4: wszystkie punkty przesunięto o ten sam wektor, więc jest to izometria.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Przystawanie i przekształcenia — Perpendicular Lines in the Plane. Nie traktuj jednokładności jako izometrii, chyba że wartość bezwzględna skali wynosi 1. Sam rysunek nie dowodzi przystawania; odwołuj się do własności lub twierdzeń.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Przystawanie i przekształcenia — Perpendicular Lines in the Plane. Opisz przekształcenie lub dane własności, zastosuj poprawny argument przystawania i uzasadnij każdy wniosek zamiast polegać na wyglądzie rysunku.

translations.title: It’s All on the Line
translations.explanation: It’s All on the Line is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Coordinate Geometry”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-CED.A.2, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales. Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point). Instructional focus: Students define variables and create equations or inequalities that model relationships among quantities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: It’s All on the Line. Define each variable with units, translate each relationship before solving, and keep the equation dimensionally and contextually consistent. Rearranging a formula must use equivalent operations.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A situation has fixed amount 27 and increases by 5 per unit. Model it by y=5x+27. At x=6, y=57. Example 2: A situation has fixed amount 16 and increases by 11 per unit. Model it by y=11x+16. At x=8, y=104.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 5x. Step 3: add fixed amount 27. Step 4: substitute x=6: y=5(6)+27=57. Step 1: define x as number of units and y as total. Step 2: variable part is 11x. Step 3: add fixed amount 16. Step 4: substitute x=8: y=11(8)+16=104.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: It’s All on the Line. Do not start manipulating symbols before stating what they mean. Avoid mixing total quantities with rates or per-unit quantities without the correct factor.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: It’s All on the Line. Define variables, translate the relationship, form an equation or inequality, and check that the model and units match the situation.

translations.title: Tworzenie równań — It’s All on the Line
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Tworzenie równań — It’s All on the Line” należy do działu „Coordinate Geometry” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:HSA-CED.A.2, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.5. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Tworzenie równań — It’s All on the Line. Definiuj każdą zmienną wraz z jednostką, najpierw przełóż relację na zapis matematyczny i zachowaj zgodność jednostek oraz kontekstu. Przy przekształcaniu wzoru stosuj działania równoważne.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Wielkość ma wartość stałą 27 i rośnie o 5 na jednostkę. Model: y=5x+27. Dla x=6, y=57. Przykład 2: Wielkość ma wartość stałą 16 i rośnie o 11 na jednostkę. Model: y=11x+16. Dla x=8, y=104.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zdefiniuj x jako liczbę jednostek, a y jako całość. Krok 2: część zmienna to 5x. Krok 3: dodaj 27. Krok 4: dla x=6: y=5(6)+27=57. Krok 1: zdefiniuj x jako liczbę jednostek, a y jako całość. Krok 2: część zmienna to 11x. Krok 3: dodaj 16. Krok 4: dla x=8: y=11(8)+16=104.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Tworzenie równań — It’s All on the Line. Nie zaczynaj przekształcać symboli, zanim nie określisz ich znaczenia. Nie mieszaj wielkości całkowitych ze stawkami jednostkowymi bez odpowiedniego czynnika.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Tworzenie równań — It’s All on the Line. Zdefiniuj zmienne, przełóż zależność na język matematyki, utwórz równanie lub nierówność i sprawdź zgodność modelu oraz jednostek z sytuacją.

translations.title: Intersection Points
translations.explanation: Intersection Points is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Coordinate Geometry”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-REI.C.7, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve a simple system consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically. For example, find the points of intersection between the line y = –3x and the circle x2 + y2 = 3. Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point). Instructional focus: Students solve equations, inequalities, and systems by using equivalent reasoning and interpreting solutions as values or intersection points. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Intersection Points. Apply the same equivalence-preserving operation to both sides. For inequalities, multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign. A solution to a system must satisfy every equation in the system.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve the system x+y=9 and x-y=-5. Adding equations gives 2x=4, so x=2; then y=7. Example 2: Solve the system x+y=9 and x-y=1. Adding equations gives 2x=10, so x=5; then y=4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=4. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=2. Step 3: substitute into x+y=9: 2+y=9, so y=7. Step 4: verify both original equations. Step 1: add the equations to eliminate y: 2x=10. Step 2: divide by 2 to get x=5. Step 3: substitute into x+y=9: 5+y=9, so y=4. Step 4: verify both original equations.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Intersection Points. Do not accept an extraneous solution created by squaring, clearing denominators, or other non-reversible steps. Verify solutions in the original relation.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Intersection Points. Transform consistently, solve, and substitute the candidate solution back into the original equation, inequality, or system.

translations.title: Rozumowanie z równaniami i nierównościami — Intersection Points
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Rozumowanie z równaniami i nierównościami — Intersection Points” należy do działu „Coordinate Geometry” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:HSA-REI.C.7, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.5. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń rozwiązuje równania, nierówności i układy przez przekształcenia równoważne oraz interpretuje rozwiązania jako wartości lub punkty przecięcia. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Rozumowanie z równaniami i nierównościami — Intersection Points. Wykonuj to samo działanie zachowujące równoważność po obu stronach. W nierówności mnożenie lub dzielenie przez liczbę ujemną odwraca znak. Rozwiązanie układu musi spełniać każde równanie.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Rozwiąż układ x+y=9 oraz x-y=-5. Po dodaniu równań: 2x=4, więc x=2; następnie y=7. Przykład 2: Rozwiąż układ x+y=9 oraz x-y=1. Po dodaniu równań: 2x=10, więc x=5; następnie y=4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: dodaj równania i wyeliminuj y: 2x=4. Krok 2: podziel przez 2: x=2. Krok 3: podstaw do x+y=9: y=7. Krok 4: sprawdź oba równania wyjściowe. Krok 1: dodaj równania i wyeliminuj y: 2x=10. Krok 2: podziel przez 2: x=5. Krok 3: podstaw do x+y=9: y=4. Krok 4: sprawdź oba równania wyjściowe.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Rozumowanie z równaniami i nierównościami — Intersection Points. Nie przyjmuj rozwiązania pozornego powstałego np. przy podnoszeniu do kwadratu lub usuwaniu mianowników. Sprawdzaj rozwiązania w relacji wyjściowej.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Rozumowanie z równaniami i nierównościami — Intersection Points. Przekształcaj konsekwentnie, rozwiąż i podstaw otrzymaną wartość do pierwotnego równania, nierówności lub układu.

translations.title: Coordinate Proof
translations.explanation: Coordinate Proof is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Coordinate Geometry”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-C.A.2, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.4, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.5, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Identify and describe relationships among inscribed angles, radii, and chords. Include the relationship between central, inscribed, and circumscribed angles; inscribed angles on a diameter are right angles; the radius of a circle is perpendicular to the tangent where the radius intersects the circle. Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically. For example, prove or disprove that a figure defined by four given points in the coordinate plane is a rectangle; prove or disprove that the point (1, √3) lies on the circle centered at the origin and containing the point (0, 2). Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point). Use coordinates to compute perimeters of polygons and areas of triangles and rectangles, e.g., using the distance formula.★ Instructional focus: Students use coordinates and algebra to describe geometric objects, prove relationships, and calculate distances, slopes, and equations. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Coordinate Proof. Slope represents direction and rate of change. Parallel nonvertical lines have equal slopes; perpendicular nonvertical lines have slopes whose product is -1. Distance and midpoint formulas follow from coordinate differences.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For A(1,1) and B(3,6), slope = (6-1)/(3-1) = 5/2. Example 2: For A(3,1) and B(6,6), slope = (6-1)/(6-3) = 5/3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: y-change is 5=5. Step 2: x-change is 2=2. Step 3: slope is 5/2=5/2. Step 4: keep the subtraction order consistent for both coordinates. Step 1: y-change is 5=5. Step 2: x-change is 3=3. Step 3: slope is 5/3=5/3. Step 4: keep the subtraction order consistent for both coordinates.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Coordinate Proof. Do not divide by zero when a line is vertical. Keep x- and y-differences paired in the same order when calculating slope.

translations.title: Weighted Averages
translations.explanation: Weighted Averages is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Coordinate Geometry”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-SSE.A.1, CCSS:HSG-CO.A.2, CCSS:HSG-GPE.B.6. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Interpret expressions that represent a quantity in terms of its context.★ a. Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients. b. Interpret complicated expressions by viewing one or more of their parts as a single entity. For example, interpret P(1+r)n as the product of P and a factor not depending on P. Represent transformations in the plane using, e.g., transparencies and geometry software; describe transformations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give other points as outputs. Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle to those that do not (e.g., translation versus horizontal stretch). Find the point on a directed line segment between two given points that partitions the segment in a given ratio. Instructional focus: Students interpret and transform algebraic expressions by recognizing terms, factors, powers, and useful structure. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Weighted Averages. Equivalent forms can reveal different features. Factoring reverses multiplication; completing a square rewrites a quadratic; exponent properties preserve value under their valid conditions.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Expand (x+6)(x+1) to get x²+7x+6; therefore x²+7x+6 factors back to (x+6)(x+1). Example 2: Expand (x+3)(x+6) to get x²+9x+18; therefore x²+9x+18 factors back to (x+3)(x+6).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: multiply x·x=x². Step 2: outer and inner terms give 1x+6x=7x. Step 3: constants give 6×1=6. Step 4: combine as x²+7x+6 and verify the factorization by re-expanding. Step 1: multiply x·x=x². Step 2: outer and inner terms give 6x+3x=9x. Step 3: constants give 3×6=18. Step 4: combine as x²+9x+18 and verify the factorization by re-expanding.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Weighted Averages. Do not combine unlike terms or cancel across addition. Check a transformed expression by expansion or substitution.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Weighted Averages. Identify the useful structure, apply an equivalence-preserving transformation, and check the new form against the original.

translations.title: A Special Point
translations.explanation: A Special Point is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Circles”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSG-CO.C.10, CCSS:HSG-CO.C.9, CCSS:HSG-SRT.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Prove theorems about triangles. Theorems include: measures of interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°; base angles of isosceles triangles are congruent; the segment joining midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half the length; the medians of a triangle meet at a point. Prove theorems about lines and angles. Theorems include: vertical angles are congruent; when a transversal crosses parallel lines, alternate interior angles are congruent and corresponding angles are congruent; points on a perpendicular bisector of a line segment are exactly those equidistant from the segment’s endpoints. Use congruence and similarity criteria for triangles to solve problems and to prove relationships in geometric figures. Instructional focus: Students reason with rigid transformations, constructions, congruence criteria, and geometric proof. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: A Special Point. Translations, rotations, and reflections preserve distance and angle measure. Congruence can be established by a sequence of rigid motions or valid triangle-congruence criteria.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Translate point P(3,1) by vector ⟨2,4⟩. The image is P′(5,5); the translation preserves distances and angle measures. Example 2: Translate point P(3,2) by vector ⟨2,5⟩. The image is P′(5,7); the translation preserves distances and angle measures.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: add 2 to the x-coordinate: 3+2=5. Step 2: add 4 to the y-coordinate: 1+4=5. Step 3: record P′(5,5). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid. Step 1: add 2 to the x-coordinate: 3+2=5. Step 2: add 5 to the y-coordinate: 2+5=7. Step 3: record P′(5,7). Step 4: note that every point moved by the same vector, so the transformation is rigid.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: A Special Point. Do not treat dilation as a rigid motion unless the scale factor has magnitude 1. A diagram alone does not prove congruence; cite preserved properties or a theorem.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: A Special Point. Describe the transformation or given properties, apply a valid congruence argument, and justify each conclusion rather than relying on appearance.

translations.title: Arcs and Sectors
translations.explanation: Arcs and Sectors is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Circles”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSA-SSE.A.1, CCSS:HSG-C.B.5, CCSS:HSG-GMD.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Interpret expressions that represent a quantity in terms of its context.★ a. Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients. b. Interpret complicated expressions by viewing one or more of their parts as a single entity. For example, interpret P(1+r)n as the product of P and a factor not depending on P. Derive using similarity the fact that the length of the arc intercepted by an angle is proportional to the radius, and define the radian measure of the angle as the constant of proportionality; derive the formula for the area of a sector. Give an informal argument for the formulas for the circumference of a circle, area of a circle, volume of a cylinder, pyramid, and cone. Use dissection arguments, Cavalieri’s principle, and informal limit arguments. Instructional focus: Students interpret and transform algebraic expressions by recognizing terms, factors, powers, and useful structure. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Arcs and Sectors. Equivalent forms can reveal different features. Factoring reverses multiplication; completing a square rewrites a quadratic; exponent properties preserve value under their valid conditions.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Expand (x+2)(x+2) to get x²+4x+4; therefore x²+4x+4 factors back to (x+2)(x+2). Example 2: Expand (x+3)(x+3) to get x²+6x+9; therefore x²+6x+9 factors back to (x+3)(x+3).
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: multiply x·x=x². Step 2: outer and inner terms give 2x+2x=4x. Step 3: constants give 2×2=4. Step 4: combine as x²+4x+4 and verify the factorization by re-expanding. Step 1: multiply x·x=x². Step 2: outer and inner terms give 3x+3x=6x. Step 3: constants give 3×3=9. Step 4: combine as x²+6x+9 and verify the factorization by re-expanding.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Arcs and Sectors. Do not combine unlike terms or cancel across addition. Check a transformed expression by expansion or substitution.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Arcs and Sectors. Identify the useful structure, apply an equivalence-preserving transformation, and check the new form against the original.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Angles, Arcs, and Radii. Area uses square units and volume uses cubic units. Scaling all lengths by k scales area by k^2 and volume by k^3. Cross-sections depend on the plane cutting the solid.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A cylinder with radius 3 and height 6 has volume V=πr²h=π(3²)(6)=54π cubic units, about 169.65. Example 2: A cylinder with radius 6 and height 10 has volume V=πr²h=π(6²)(10)=360π cubic units, about 1130.97.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify radius r=3 and height h=6. Step 2: square the radius: 3²=9. Step 3: multiply by height: 9×6=54. Step 4: volume is 54π≈169.65 cubic units. Step 1: identify radius r=6 and height h=10. Step 2: square the radius: 6²=36. Step 3: multiply by height: 36×10=360. Step 4: volume is 360π≈1130.97 cubic units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Angles, Arcs, and Radii. Do not use a surface-area formula when volume is requested. Track whether a dimension is radius or diameter and keep units consistent.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Angles, Arcs, and Radii. Identify the geometric quantity and dimensions, apply the appropriate formula or scaling relationship, calculate, and state squared or cubed units correctly.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: A New Way to Measure Angles. Equivalent forms can reveal different features. Factoring reverses multiplication; completing a square rewrites a quadratic; exponent properties preserve value under their valid conditions.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Expand (x+7)(x+6) to get x²+13x+42; therefore x²+13x+42 factors back to (x+7)(x+6). Example 2: Expand (x+6)(x+1) to get x²+7x+6; therefore x²+7x+6 factors back to (x+6)(x+1).

translations.title: Playing with Probability
translations.explanation: Playing with Probability is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Conditional Probability”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSS-CP.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Describe events as subsets of a sample space (the set of outcomes) using characteristics (or categories) of the outcomes, or as unions, intersections, or complements of other events (“or,” “and,” “not”). The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Playing with Probability. P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. Independent events satisfy P(A|B)=P(A). Use complements, unions, intersections, permutations, or combinations according to the event structure.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Among 63 outcomes, event B occurs in 53 and both A and B occur in 43. Then P(A|B)=43/53≈0.811. Example 2: Among 51 outcomes, event B occurs in 25 and both A and B occur in 10. Then P(A|B)=10/25≈0.400.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: condition on B, reducing the relevant sample space to 53 outcomes. Step 2: within B, 43 outcomes also satisfy A. Step 3: divide 43 by 53 to get 0.811. Step 4: confirm the probability lies between 0 and 1. Step 1: condition on B, reducing the relevant sample space to 25 outcomes. Step 2: within B, 10 outcomes also satisfy A. Step 3: divide 10 by 25 to get 0.400. Step 4: confirm the probability lies between 0 and 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Playing with Probability. Do not confuse mutually exclusive with independent events. In conditional probability, restrict the sample space to the condition before forming the ratio.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Playing with Probability. Define the events and sample space, choose the appropriate counting or probability rule, calculate, and interpret the probability in context.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń analizuje zdarzenia złożone, niezależność, prawdopodobieństwo warunkowe i reguły zliczania przy jasno określonej przestrzeni zdarzeń. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Prawdopodobieństwo warunkowe — Sample Spaces. P(A|B)=P(A i B)/P(B), gdy P(B)>0. Dla zdarzeń niezależnych P(A|B)=P(A). Stosuj dopełnienia, sumy i części wspólne zdarzeń oraz permutacje lub kombinacje zgodnie ze strukturą sytuacji.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Wśród 54 wyników zdarzenie B zachodzi w 26, a A i B jednocześnie w 10. Zatem P(A|B)=10/26≈0.385. Przykład 2: Wśród 80 wyników zdarzenie B zachodzi w 31, a A i B jednocześnie w 15. Zatem P(A|B)=15/31≈0.484.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: warunek B ogranicza przestrzeń do 26 wyników. Krok 2: spośród nich 10 spełnia także A. Krok 3: 10/26≈0.385. Krok 4: wynik musi leżeć między 0 i 1. Krok 1: warunek B ogranicza przestrzeń do 31 wyników. Krok 2: spośród nich 15 spełnia także A. Krok 3: 15/31≈0.484. Krok 4: wynik musi leżeć między 0 i 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Prawdopodobieństwo warunkowe — Sample Spaces. Nie myl zdarzeń rozłącznych z niezależnymi. W prawdopodobieństwie warunkowym najpierw ogranicz przestrzeń zdarzeń do warunku, a dopiero potem twórz iloraz.

translations.title: Tables of Relative Frequencies
translations.explanation: Tables of Relative Frequencies is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Conditional Probability”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSS-CP.A.4, CCSS:HSS-ID.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities. For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected student from your school will favor science given that the student is in tenth grade. Do the same for other subjects and compare the results. Summarize categorical data for two categories in two-way frequency tables. Interpret relative frequencies in the context of the data (including joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies). Recognize possible associations and trends in the data. Instructional focus: Students analyze compound events, independence, conditional probability, and counting rules using clearly defined sample spaces. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Tables of Relative Frequencies. P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. Independent events satisfy P(A|B)=P(A). Use complements, unions, intersections, permutations, or combinations according to the event structure.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Among 54 outcomes, event B occurs in 38 and both A and B occur in 29. Then P(A|B)=29/38≈0.763. Example 2: Among 44 outcomes, event B occurs in 33 and both A and B occur in 25. Then P(A|B)=25/33≈0.758.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: condition on B, reducing the relevant sample space to 38 outcomes. Step 2: within B, 29 outcomes also satisfy A. Step 3: divide 29 by 38 to get 0.763. Step 4: confirm the probability lies between 0 and 1. Step 1: condition on B, reducing the relevant sample space to 33 outcomes. Step 2: within B, 25 outcomes also satisfy A. Step 3: divide 25 by 33 to get 0.758. Step 4: confirm the probability lies between 0 and 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Tables of Relative Frequencies. Do not confuse mutually exclusive with independent events. In conditional probability, restrict the sample space to the condition before forming the ratio.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Tables of Relative Frequencies. Define the events and sample space, choose the appropriate counting or probability rule, calculate, and interpret the probability in context.

translations.title: Related Events
translations.explanation: Related Events is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Conditional Probability”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSS-CP.A.2, CCSS:HSS-CP.A.4, CCSS:HSS-CP.A.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that two events A and B are independent if the probability of A and B occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if they are independent. Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities. For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected student from your school will favor science given that the student is in tenth grade. Do the same for other subjects and compare the results. Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations. For example, compare the chance of having lung cancer if you are a smoker with the chance of being a smoker if you have lung cancer. Instructional focus: Students analyze compound events, independence, conditional probability, and counting rules using clearly defined sample spaces. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.title: Using Tables for Conditional Probability
translations.explanation: Using Tables for Conditional Probability is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Conditional Probability”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSS-CP.A.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities. For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected student from your school will favor science given that the student is in tenth grade. Do the same for other subjects and compare the results. Instructional focus: Students analyze compound events, independence, conditional probability, and counting rules using clearly defined sample spaces. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Using Tables for Conditional Probability. P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. Independent events satisfy P(A|B)=P(A). Use complements, unions, intersections, permutations, or combinations according to the event structure.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Among 42 outcomes, event B occurs in 26 and both A and B occur in 13. Then P(A|B)=13/26≈0.500. Example 2: Among 59 outcomes, event B occurs in 28 and both A and B occur in 17. Then P(A|B)=17/28≈0.607.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: condition on B, reducing the relevant sample space to 26 outcomes. Step 2: within B, 13 outcomes also satisfy A. Step 3: divide 13 by 26 to get 0.500. Step 4: confirm the probability lies between 0 and 1. Step 1: condition on B, reducing the relevant sample space to 28 outcomes. Step 2: within B, 17 outcomes also satisfy A. Step 3: divide 17 by 28 to get 0.607. Step 4: confirm the probability lies between 0 and 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Using Tables for Conditional Probability. Do not confuse mutually exclusive with independent events. In conditional probability, restrict the sample space to the condition before forming the ratio.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Using Tables for Conditional Probability. Define the events and sample space, choose the appropriate counting or probability rule, calculate, and interpret the probability in context.

translations.title: Using Probability to Determine Whether Events Are Independent

It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSS-CP.A.3, CCSS:HSS-CP.A.4, CCSS:HSS-CP.A.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), and interpret independence of A and B as saying that the conditional probability of A given B is the same as the probability of A, and the conditional probability of B given A is the same as the probability of B. Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities. For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected student from your school will favor science given that the student is in tenth grade. Do the same for other subjects and compare the results. Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations. For example, compare the chance of having lung cancer if you are a smoker with the chance of being a smoker if you have lung cancer. Instructional focus: Students analyze compound events, independence, conditional probability, and counting rules using clearly defined sample spaces. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.title: Probabilities in Games
translations.explanation: Probabilities in Games is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Conditional Probability”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:HSS-CP.A.2, CCSS:HSS-CP.A.3, CCSS:HSS-CP.A.5, CCSS:HSS-CP.B.6. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that two events A and B are independent if the probability of A and B occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if they are independent. Understand the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), and interpret independence of A and B as saying that the conditional probability of A given B is the same as the probability of A, and the conditional probability of B given A is the same as the probability of B. Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations. For example, compare the chance of having lung cancer if you are a smoker with the chance of being a smoker if you have lung cancer. Find the conditional probability of A given B as the fraction of B’s outcomes that also belong to A, and interpret the answer in terms of the model. Instructional focus: Students analyze compound events, independence, conditional probability, and counting rules using clearly defined sample spaces. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Among 69 outcomes, event B occurs in 58 and both A and B occur in 20. Then P(A|B)=20/58≈0.345. Example 2: Among 50 outcomes, event B occurs in 38 and both A and B occur in 31. Then P(A|B)=31/38≈0.816.

Step 4: confirm the probability lies between 0 and 1. Step 1: condition on B, reducing the relevant sample space to 38 outcomes. Step 2: within B, 31 outcomes also satisfy A.
